The stripe-faced dunnart (Sminthopsis macroura) is a small, insectivorous dasyurid marsupial native to arid and semi-arid regions of Australia. This species exhibits extreme physiological flexibility to cope with unpredictable environmental conditions, including the capacity for daily torpor, which substantially reduces metabolic demands. Basal metabolic measurements are typically collected under controlled thermal conditions, with standard metabolic trials conducted at a body temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], which approximates the normothermic active phase for this species. Newborn young, termed pups, are altricial at birth and extremely small, with each neonate weighing just 0.01 grams [Wwb = 0.01 grams] at delivery. This minuscule birth mass reflects the marsupial pattern of a brief gestation followed by a prolonged period of postnatal development within the maternal pouch, where the developing joey must latch onto a teat for continuous nutrition. The extreme altriciality of the neonates places a significant energetic burden on the lactating female, who must sustain a high metabolic output to provision rapidly growing young throughout the critical early developmental window.

Reproduction in the stripe-faced dunnart is tightly linked to resource availability, with breeding typically concentrated in the spring and summer months when insect prey is most abundant. At a stable body temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], the gestation period lasts approximately 14 days [tg = approximately 14 days], which is comparatively brief even among dasyurid marsupials and allows females to quickly capitalize on favorable environmental conditions. Following parturition, the altricial neonates, still resembling tiny embryos, migrate unaided to the pouch where they attach permanently to a teat for the duration of early development. Females typically produce two litters per year [F_R_i = two litters per year], though some field observations suggest that a third litter may be possible in particularly productive seasons. Each litter comprises about 8 pups [N_R_i = Each litter comprises about 8 pups], resulting in a substantial annual reproductive output for a small mammal, though high early mortality rates mean that only a fraction of these individuals typically survive to independence.

The postnatal development of the stripe-faced dunnart follows a well-defined trajectory that is intimately linked to the mother's metabolic investment. Because all developmental milestones are measured at the species' characteristic normothermic body temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], the timing of these events is highly predictable under stable conditions. The time since birth at weaning averages 67 days since birth [tx = 67 days since birth], though this can vary within a range of 65 to 70 days depending on maternal condition and litter size at a temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. Weaning marks the nutritional independence of the juveniles and the cessation of lactation, after which the young must begin foraging for arthropod prey on their own. At the point of weaning, the typical wet weight of the offspring is approximately 7 grams [Wwx = approximately 7 grams], representing a substantial increase from the negligible birth mass but still far below adult dimensions. This intermediate body size necessitates a period of rapid somatic growth and intensive foraging before the individuals can attain the mass required for reproductive maturation.

Sexual maturation in the stripe-faced dunnart occurs relatively quickly following weaning, consistent with the species' opportunistic life history strategy suited to unpredictable arid environments. At a core body temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 122 days since birth [tp = approximately 122 days since birth], reflecting the interval required for the completion of gonadal development and the onset of gametogenesis. This relatively early maturation allows individuals born in the early breeding season to potentially reproduce within the same calendar year, contributing to the species' capacity for rapid population increase during favorable conditions. The adult body mass, or ultimate wet weight, of a fully grown stripe-faced dunnart averages around 20 grams [Wwi = around 20 grams], though healthy individuals in the field typically range from 15 to 25 grams depending on sex, season, and local resource abundance. This modest adult size places the species among the smaller members of the genus Sminthopsis, and the relatively high surface-area-to-volume ratio imposes significant thermoregulatory challenges in the extreme thermal environment of the Australian outback.

Longevity in the stripe-faced dunnart is constrained by the high metabolic costs of small body size, intense reproductive effort, and the physiological demands of surviving in a harsh, variable environment. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 4.9 years [am = approximately 4.9 years], which is equivalent to roughly 1789 days. In the wild, actual longevity is likely considerably shorter due to predation, resource limitation, and the high energetic costs of reproduction, with most individuals probably surviving no more than one or two breeding seasons. This lifespan is broadly consistent with that of other small dasyurid marsupials of comparable adult body mass, reflecting a general life-history pattern in which small, short-lived mammals prioritize early and rapid reproduction over extended somatic maintenance. The ability to enter daily torpor during cold periods or food scarcity likely provides an important mechanism for extending the operational lifespan by reducing cumulative metabolic damage and conserving limited endogenous energy reserves.
